source.title: The Geometry of Thought: How Scale Restructures Reasoning In Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws but measures reasoning-trajectory geometry, not held-out cross-entropy, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture effects at fixed parameter count, or downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss. Its geometric results do not test a listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports geometric measurements across domains and two model scales. These results concern a related but different outcome from the claim versions, so they are recorded with versions ["none"]. Its 63.6% probe-decoding result also does not measure downstream performance scaling or prediction from pretraining loss. The paper's discussion of prior loss-scaling results is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann and calls its results 'domain-dependent scaling laws'. Its own measurements, though, are hidden-state trajectory geometry (d95, G/L ratio, alignment, silhouette, coherence) for two Llama instruct models (8B, 70B). It reports no held-out loss, no compute or token sweeps, no fixed-size architecture comparison, and no task accuracy at either scale. None of its results bear on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that scale restructures reasoning geometry in domain-specific ways: Law 'crystallizes', Science and Math stay invariant, and Code forms clusters. They also report a universal coherence of about −0.4. They argue that aggregate scaling curves may average over these heterogeneous effects, but they measure no loss or accuracy scaling. They also claim that geometry predicts operator learnability, based on an 8B-only pilot reaching 63.6% probe accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures hidden-state trajectory geometry and trains endpoint-prediction operators; it does not use the original studies' held-out-loss scaling sweeps or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Domain changes the reported geometric outcomes; the paper reports different patterns across Law, Science, Code, and Math. Only two scales, 8B and 70B, are tested.

fits_no_version.finding: Between Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, CoT hidden-state geometry changes by domain. Law: d95 501→274, G/L 9.82→0.98, alignment 0.72→0.94, silhouette 0.07→0.26. Science: d95 237→235. Math: d95 501→501, G/L 9.82 at both scales. Code: silhouette 0.133→0.417, G/L about 1.1 at both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-trajectory geometry changes with model scale in domain-specific rather than uniform ways.

fits_no_version.finding: Step-to-step coherence of consecutive hidden-state velocity vectors is about −0.40 to −0.42 in all four domains at both scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CoT hidden-state trajectories in Llama models show similar negative (oscillatory) step-to-step coherence across domains and scales.

record.code_released: The authors say they will release the extraction, geometry analysis, and operator/probe training code upon acceptance; until then, materials are available to qualified researchers upon request. No URL stated.
record.problems: Only one model family is tested; only two scale points are compared, so the scaling-function shape cannot be characterized. The domains use different datasets and differ in dataset size, problem difficulty, and answer format. The paper itself notes that the observed associations do not establish causation. No held-out loss-scaling results are reported for the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were left out for the 60-row limit. The paper also describes intrinsic-dimension ranges, compactness, normalized heatmap metrics, cluster counts, and alignment changes for Science, Code, and Math; exact per-model values are not all stated in text or are only shown in figures, so they were not added as model-specific numeric rows.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of fitted power laws to larger runs.
No fixed-parameter architecture comparisons; the 8B and 70B models differ in size.
No power-law fits in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream accuracy reported for 8B versus 70B, and no prediction of it from loss; the geometry metrics are not task performance.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons. With two scale points, curve shape cannot be assessed, as the authors state.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling laws' loosely for an 8B-versus-70B comparison across different model versions (Llama-3 versus 3.1), which differ in more than parameter count. Figure 9 reports alignment deltas with 95% CIs: Science +0.15, Code +0.18, Math −0.01. These are not rows but are geometry, so they are irrelevant to V1–V7. The remaining rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocation at fixed compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance scaling or its predictability from pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting and setup choices, or curvature in loss-scaling curves.

rows.note: The paper says this exceeded baselines by 10 percentage points. The pilot is discussed as CaseHOLD-based; this does not test downstream performance scaling.
rows.check: This is the study's own endpoint operator (Turbo) compared with baselines on the 8B CaseHOLD pilot. It is the study's method performance, not a measurement of model behaviour across scale, and should not be a result row. The baseline value is not stated, only '10 percentage points' above it.
